::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Visualizing the flow of a constant vector field: shouldn't all the flow lines (integral curves) be in the same direction as the vector field?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3395589/visualizing-the-flow-of-a-constant-vector-field-shouldnt-all-the-flow-lines-i), asked by [James Ronald](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/598227/james-ronald) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2019-10-16; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> A question in my text proposes the vector field $\vec v = x\vec j$. It shows that this: 
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
>
> as being the field itself; this makes sense. It also shows $\vec v$
> 's flow as being this:
>
> [![enter image description here][q-2]][q-2]
>
>
>   [q-1]: tequq.png
>   [q-2]: klSF7.png
>
> Why is it that all the flow lines are in the same direction? Shouldn't the ones in quadrants $2$ and $3$, where $x$ is negative, be pointing/flowing downwards?
:::

I agree with you.  The flow line through $(x_0,y_0)$ has equations $x(t) = x_0$, $y(t) = y_0 + x_0t$.
